title: Engineering multi-photon dissipation with a dc-voltage-biased Josephson junction
authors: Marco Paradina, Ambroise Peugeot, Roberto Negrin, Oscar Novat, Tristan Villain, Anil Murani, Jean-Loup Ville, Sébastien Jezouin, Raphaël Lescanne, Audrey Bienfait, Benjamin Huard
abstract: Multi-photon dissipation -- a key resource for bosonic qubits -- is usually realized by parametrically pumping a Josephson coupler at the cost of spurious nonlinear terms. Here we instead engineer it using a dc-voltage-biased SQUID, such that these parasitic terms average out. We activate the conversion of one, two, or four photons of a high-Q mode into a single photon of a lossy mode. We characterize the two-photon dissipation by Wigner tomography, establishing dc-biased junctions as a resource for reservoir engineering and a viable route to cat-qubit stabilization.
summary: The authors demonstrate a novel method to engineer multi-photon dissipation in superconducting circuits by biasing a SQUID junction with a DC voltage. This technique allows for precise control over photon loss rates, enabling the study of bosonic qubits and providing a robust pathway for stabilizing complex quantum states like cat qubits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of engineering multi-photon dissipation, a crucial resource for bosonic qubits, by developing a method that avoids spurious nonlinear terms present in standard parametric pumping techniques.
main_result: They successfully demonstrated that using a dc-voltage-biased SQUID can engineer controlled single- and two-photon loss, and activate up to 4-to-1 photon swaps, proving it is a viable route for reservoir engineering and cat-qubit stabilization.
method: The research combines microwave reflectometry to characterize coupling strengths and voltage sweeping to activate specific photon conversion processes, complemented by Wigner tomography to measure the time evolution of the quantum state.
model_or_system: The physical system is a superconducting circuit comprising a high-Q memory resonator coupled to a buffer resonator via a dc-voltage-biased SQUID. The dynamics are modeled using a Josephson Hamiltonian and analyzed via a master equation incorporating dissipation terms.
key_observables: Two-photon dissipation rate ($\kappa_2$), single-photon loss rate ($\kappa_a$), photon number decay $ ar{n}(	au)$, and the Wigner function $W( eta)$.
important_parameters: The engineered dissipation rate $\kappa_2$ is proportional to the buffer loss rate $\kappa_b$; the coupling strength $g_{	ext{max}}^2/2\pi$ was measured to be $18.5 \pm 0.5$ MHz.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on adiabatically eliminating the buffer mode and assumes that parasitic nonlinear terms average out to zero at first order in the rotating wave approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate energy level diagrams showing photon conversion, circuit schematics, and time-domain plots ($ ar{n}(	au)$) comparing decay under different loss mechanisms (e.g., 1-photon vs. 2-photon loss).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform and the theoretical advantage of the dc-bias method, to characterizing various photon swap regimes (1-to-1, 2-to-1, 4-to-1) via reflectometry, and finally quantifying the dissipation dynamics using time-resolved Wigner tomography.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable, solid-state platform for implementing engineered dissipation, which is fundamental for building robust quantum memories and stabilizing high-dimensional quantum states like cat qubits.
